claims.text: The test specimens begin as a single-phase BCC or FCC solid solution with no detectable secondary phases.
Combined cyclic mechanical loading and thermal cycling nucleates nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries.
Elevated-temperature loading in oxygen produces oxygen-induced segregation or other embrittling features at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary precipitates or oxygen-induced features degrade grain-boundary cohesion.
The proposed grain-boundary features suppress plastic deformation mechanisms.
Suppression of plastic deformation reduces intrinsic toughening and resistance to crack initiation and growth.
Plasticity is a principal intrinsic toughening mechanism in ductile materials.
Loss of plastic deformation promotes a transition to brittle, intergranular crack propagation.
Fracture plasticity can diminish as temperature rises in a high-entropy alloy, potentially because of high-temperature oxidation.
Specimens subjected to cyclic high-temperature loading will have lower fracture toughness than specimens tested quasi-statically at room temperature.
After cyclic high-temperature loading, SEM or TEM will reveal grain-boundary precipitates or oxygen-induced embrittling features.
After cyclic high-temperature loading, fracture surfaces will show intergranular rather than ductile dimple features.
The room-temperature, quasi-static baseline exhibits ductile fracture, extensive plastic deformation, and dimpled fracture surfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 873–1073 K under cyclic or high-rate loading when oxygen can interact with the alloy.
Extremely low temperatures or purely inert atmospheres may not produce the proposed precipitation- or oxidation-mediated embrittlement.
The composition, size, distribution, kinetics, and embrittlement onset of the proposed features vary with alloy composition and oxygen level.
